'''Eva J. Pell''' (born March 11, 1948) is a biologist, plant pathologist, and science administrator. Pell's research focused on the physiological and biochemical impacts of air pollutants on vegetation. As a science administrator at [[Pennsylvania State University]] and the [[Smithsonian Institution]], Dr. Pell initiated several pan-institutional science institutes. Since leaving the Smithsonian, she is developing a series of adventure stories for elementary school children with the theme rescuing endangered species.

== Early life and education ==
Eva Joy Pell was born in [[New York, New York]]. She earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] in biology from [[City College of New York]] in 1968 and a Ph.D. in plant biology from [[Rutgers University]] in 1972.<ref name="Business Week">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Eva J. Pell: Executive Profile |url=http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/private/person.asp?personId=6138389 |newspaper=[[Bloomberg Businessweek]] |location=[[New York City]] |publisher=[[Bloomberg L.P.]] |accessdate=28 March 2014}}{{dead link|date=April 2023|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

== Career ==
Eva J. Pell was appointed as assistant professor of Plant Pathology at the [[Pennsylvania State University]] in 1973. In 1991, she was named Distinguished Professor of Plant Pathology and in 1995, was named the John and [[Nancy Steimer]] Professor of Agricultural Sciences.<ref name="Pell Alumni Award">{{cite web|title=Honorary Alumni Awards|url=http://alumni.psu.edu/awards/individual/honorary/docs/2011-honorary/2011-HA-EPell.pdf|publisher=Pennsylvania State Alumni Association|accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref>

Pell's research focused on the physiological and biochemical impacts of air pollutants on vegetation, and her research spanned from the molecular to the ecophysiological.<ref name="House Rep">{{cite web |title=Eva J. Pell: Under Secretary for Science |url=http://docs.house.gov/meetings/SY/SY15/20140114/101640/HHRG-113-SY15-Bio-PellE-20140114.pdf |publisher=[[U.S. House of Representatives]] |accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref> Her work examined several pollutants – [[sulfur dioxide]], acid rain, and ozone – and she is known for her study of the mechanism for ozone-induced accelerated leaf senescence (aging).<ref>{{cite journal|last=Pell|first=Eva J.|author2=Bryan W. Brendley|author3=Judith P. Sinn|title=OZONE-INDUCED ACCELERATED FOLIAR SENESCENCE: IMPLICATIONS FOR TOXICITY AND COMPENSATION|journal=Gen. Tech. Rep. NE-214. Radnor, PA: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Northeastern Forest Experiment Station.|year=1996|pages=13–19|url=http://www.nrs.fs.fed.us/pubs/gtr/gtr_ne214/gtr_ne214_013.pdf|accessdate=20 March 2014|archive-date=1 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170501165856/https://www.nrs.fs.fed.us/pubs/gtr/gtr_ne214/gtr_ne214_013.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>  She is the author or co-author of more than 100 publications and 65 abstracts.<ref name="Penn State News - Research Facility">{{cite web|title=Penn State research facility named for Eva J. Pell|url=http://news.psu.edu/story/155611/2011/09/09/penn-state-research-facility-named-eva-j-pell|publisher=Pennsylvania State University|accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref>

Pell's career as a science administrator began on July 1, 1999, when she was appointed Interim Vice President of Research at [[Pennsylvania State University]], which she served until January 2000. In January 2000, Dr. Pell was appointed vice president for Research and Dean of the Graduate School at Pennsylvania State University. On May 12, 2006, her title was changed to Senior Vice President for Research and Dean of the Graduate School, a position she held until December 31, 2009.<ref name="House Rep" />

In her role as Senior Vice President for Research, Pell spearheaded the development of cross-disciplinary institutes for life sciences, materials, energy and environment, social sciences, cyber science, and arts and humanities. She oversaw the full development of the Huck Institutes for the Life Sciences,<ref>{{cite web|title=Report of the Interdisciplinary Task Force|url=https://www.aau.edu/WorkArea/DownloadAsset.aspx?id=462|publisher=Association of American Universities|accessdate=20 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141103124938/http://aau.edu/WorkArea/DownloadAsset.aspx?id=462|archive-date=2014-11-03|url-status=dead}}</ref> the Materials Research Institute, the Social Science Research Institute,<ref>{{cite web|title=Interdisciplinary Research Focus Bearing Fruit, Places Penn State at Forefront of National Trend |url=http://www.psu.edu/ur/2002/interdisciplinaryresearch.html|publisher=Pennsylvania State University|accessdate=20 March 2014}}</ref> the Penn State Institutes for Energy and the Environment, and the Institute for CyberScience.<ref>{{cite web|title=About the Institute for CyberScience|url=https://www.ics.psu.edu/about/index.html|publisher=Penn State Institute for CyberScience|accessdate=20 March 2014|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140409175335/http://www.ics.psu.edu/about/index.html|archivedate=9 April 2014}}</ref>  An outgrowth of that effort included Eva championing the construction of the state-of-the art Millennium Science Complex, home to the Huck Institutes for the Life Sciences and the Materials Research Institute.<ref>{{cite web|title=Growth in research funding can spur innovation, economic development|url=http://news.psu.edu/story/181348/2008/12/01/growth-research-funding-can-spur-innovation-economic-development|work=Penn State News|publisher=Pennsylvania State University|accessdate=20 March 2014|archive-date=25 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130925082705/http://news.psu.edu/story/181348/2008/12/01/growth-research-funding-can-spur-innovation-economic-development|url-status=dead}}</ref> All six institutes reported directly to her.  She was also responsible for sponsored research, compliance and the university's animal research center. In addition, Pell was responsible for the Penn State Research and Technology Transfer Organization, which connects Penn State researchers with industries in order to stimulate economic development.<ref name="SI Newsdesk Bio">{{cite web|title=Newsdesk Staff Biographies: Eva J. Pell|url=http://newsdesk.si.edu/about/bios/eva-pell|publisher=Smithsonian Institution|accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref> Pell was active in economic development and served on numerous state boards including the Ben Franklin Center of Central and Northern Pennsylvania, the Ben Franklin Technology Development Authority, the Technology Collaborative and the Life Science Greenhouse for Central Pennsylvania. She was also President of the Penn State Research Foundation and the Research Park Management Corp.<ref name="Business Week" />

As dean of the Penn State Graduate School, Pell oversaw graduate admissions, fellowships, awards, and curriculum and developed several programs at Penn State to increase the number of minority applicants for graduate programs.<ref name="SI Newsdesk Bio" />

Pell's term in the Penn State research office saw a nearly two-fold increase in research expenditures from US$393 million to US$765 million in 2009.<ref name="Pell Alumni Award" />  According to the [[National Science Foundation]], Penn State ranked ninth nationally among all public and private universities in science and engineering Research & Development expenditures.<ref>{{cite web|title=R&D expenditures at universities and colleges|url=https://www.nsf.gov/statistics/nsf11313/pdf/tab31.pdf|publisher=National Science Foundation|accessdate=19 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130113031903/http://www.nsf.gov/statistics/nsf11313/pdf/tab31.pdf|archive-date=13 January 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On September 9, 2011, the Penn State Board of Trustees on Friday approved the naming of a new lab building as the "Eva J. Pell Laboratory for Advance Biological Research." The 20,000-square-foot building was designed to support immunology and infectious disease research.<ref name="Penn State News - Research Facility" />

Pell worked for Penn State for 36 years before leaving to work as the Under Secretary for Science at the [[Smithsonian Institution]] on Jan. 4, 2010.<ref>{{cite web|title=Eva Pell Named Smithsonian Under Secretary for Science|url=http://newsdesk.si.edu/releases/eva-pell-named-smithsonian-under-secretary-science|publisher=Smithsonian Institution|accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref>  In her role at the Smithsonian, she oversaw the operations of the [[National Museum of Natural History]]; the [[National Air and Space Museum]]; the [[National Zoological Park (United States)|National Zoo]] and its Conservation and Research Center in Front Royal, Va.; the [[Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory]] in Cambridge, Mass.; the [[Smithsonian Environmental Research Center]] in Edgewater, Md.; the Smithsonian's [[Museum Conservation Institute]] in Suitland, Md.; and the [[Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute]] in Panama.<ref name="SI Newsdesk Bio" />

During Pell's tenure at the Smithsonian, The Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute's opened a state-of-the-art genetics lab at the National Zoo in Washington, D.C.<ref>{{cite web|title=Smithsonian's National Zoo Opens New Genetics Lab|url=http://newsdesk.si.edu/releases/smithsonian-s-national-zoo-opens-new-genetics-lab|publisher=Smithsonian Institution|accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref> Also, in October 2012, the Smithsonian announced the formation of the Tennenbaum Marine Observatories Network.<ref>{{cite web|title=Emmett Duffy Named Director of Smithsonian's Tennenbaum Marine Observatories Network|url=http://newsdesk.si.edu/releases/emmett-duffy-named-director-smithsonian-s-tennenbaum-marine-observatories-network|publisher=Smithsonian Institution|accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref>  The project will be the first worldwide network of coastal ecological field sites with the goal of standardizing measurements of biological change.

Pell retired from the [[Smithsonian Institution]] in March, 2014.<ref>{{cite web|title=Eva Pell to Step Down As Smithsonian's Under Secretary for Science|url=http://newsdesk.si.edu/releases/eva-pell-step-down-smithsonian-s-under-secretary-science|publisher=Smithsonian Institution|accessdate=19 March 2014}}</ref> In September 2019, Pell released the first in a series of adventure novels about rescuing endangered species for children ages 9–12, titled ''ResQ and the Baby Orangutan''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://radio.wpsu.org/post/take-note-former-penn-state-research-vp-pens-childrens-book|title=Take Note: Former Penn State Research VP Pens Children's Book|last=Danahy|first=Anne|website=radio.wpsu.org|date=4 October 2019 |language=en|access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref> The second book in the series, ''ResQ Takes on the Takhi'', was published in 2020, and the third book, ''ResQ in Panamá: Can We Save The Frogs?'', in 2022.

== Personal life ==
Eva J. Pell is married to Ira Pell. They have two grown daughters, Erika Pell '98 Penn State, and Rachel Pell '00 Penn State, and three grandchildren.<ref name="Pell Alumni Award" />
